commentary.seminaVerbi:
Isaiah’s “called from the womb” has the feel of a vocation that precedes consent, like the Daoist sense of being borne along by a prior Way, or the Hindu idea of svadharma pressing up from one’s own nature; speculation: it reads like identity as discovery rather than construction. The “mouth like a sharp sword” matches the Zen and Chan suspicion that true speech cuts—katsu, the shout that cleaves delusion—while also resembling the Sikh insistence that the tongue can be kirpan, a blade for truth without blood. The ache of “laboured in vain” is close to the Bhagavad Gita’s counsel to release the fruit, and to Stoic discipline: do the work, surrender the outcome. “Light of the Gentiles” echoes the bodhisattva vow to turn outward beyond one’s own clan, and the Islamic intuition of a mercy meant for all worlds; speculation: the text imagines universality as an expansion of intimacy, not an erasure of origin.

In Luke, the fight over the name is a psychological rupture with the family script, like Buddhist renunciation of inherited roles or the Sufi break from tribal identity into a new nisba, a new belonging. The father’s silence and sudden speech resembles the yogic motif of mauna ripening into utterance, or the prophetic pattern in many traditions where speech is withheld until it can serve something larger than self-display. The child’s desert formation parallels the forest-dweller stage in Hinduism and the hermit training in early Buddhism: solitude as the furnace where a public voice is tempered; speculation: the wilderness here is less geography than a deliberate unmaking of social noise so a truer name can be heard.
commentary.excursus:
Isaiah’s “called from the womb” is not comfort but conscription. The mouth as “sharp sword” is a violence turned inward first: speech that cuts the speaker, a life hidden like an arrow in a quiver, stored for impact. The servant is renamed “Israel” and then immediately confesses futility—worked to exhaustion “without cause.” This is the psychology of being chosen and still feeling useless, the dread that destiny is just a grander stage for failure. The pivot to “light of the Gentiles” reads like escalation, not mercy: when the local mission collapses, the demand expands to the ends of the earth, as if bigness could anesthetize shame.

Luke answers with a domestic scene that curdles into omen. The neighbors want continuity—call him by his father’s name—because names keep families intact. Elizabeth refuses, and the father, mute until he submits in writing, is released into speech only when the old identity is severed. The community’s “congratulations” flip to fear: they sense that this child is not a gift to them but a rupture in them. John’s first belonging is to a name that fits no kinship, and his growth ends not in the village but in the desert, the place where desire is stripped to raw appetite and dread. He is the arrow kept hidden, not because he is precious, but because he is dangerous.
commentary.synthesis: God names and commissions before visibility, and his word overrules kinship and custom. The servant’s apparent futility is the prelude to a mission that exceeds Israel and reaches the nations.

gospel.text: The narrative moves from private mercy to public rumor to communal interpretation. Wonder and fear function as social recognition that a birth has become a sign; the question about the child’s future is generated by perceived divine agency (“hand of the Lord”), not by pedigree or expectation.

reading.text: The speaker is both “servant Israel” and the one tasked to restore Israel: a deliberate compression of person and people. The mission is framed as pre-temporal formation, then re-framed as apparent failure, then re-authorized by God’s own valuation—glory and strength are assigned from above, not inferred from outcomes.

marginalia.text: Called before speech; named before achievement.
Vocation feels like waste; appeal is to the Judge, not the crowd.
Israel’s repair is “small”; the horizon is planetary.
Rite meets custom: the community tries to name what it can control.
Writing breaks the stalemate; the name arrives as decree.
Silence ends when the word is submitted to.
Strength is forged offstage; manifestation is scheduled.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, who raised up Saint John the Baptist to prepare for Christ the Lord a people well disposed, grant to your family the gift of spiritual joy, and guide the will of your children along the path of salvation and peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:
Lord Jesus Christ, you are meek and humble of heart and you offer those who come to you a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light; deign, then, to accept the desires and the deeds of the day we have ended. May we rest during the night, so that, with body and spirit renewed, we may persevere steadfastly in your service. You who live and reign for ever and ever.

lines: Give ear, ye islands, and hearken, ye people from afar. The Lord hath called me from the womb, from the bowels of my mother he hath been mindful of my name.
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword: in the shadow of his hand he hath protected me, and hath made me as a chosen arrow: in his quiver he hath hidden me.
And he said to me: Thou art my servant Israel, for in thee will I glory.
And I said: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength without cause and in vain: therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.

And now saith the Lord, that formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I may bring back Jacob unto him, and Israel will not be gathered together: and I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God is made my strength.

And he said: It is a small thing that thou shouldst be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to convert the dregs of Israel. Behold, I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles, that thou mayst be my salvation even to the farthest part of the earth.

lines: Now Elizabeth's full time of being delivered was come: and she brought forth a son.
And her neighbors and kinsfolks heard that the Lord had shewed his great mercy towards her: and they congratulated with her.
And it came to pass that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child: and they called him by his father's name Zachary.
And his mother answering, said: Not so. But he shall be called John.
And they said to her: There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.
And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called.
And demanding a writing table, he wrote, saying: John is his name. And they all wondered.
And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed: and he spoke, blessing God.
And fear came upon all their neighbours: and all these things were noised abroad over all the hill country of Judea.
And all they that had heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: What an one, think ye, shall this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.
And the child grew and was strengthened in spirit: and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.
